screens.title: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure as Code is the practice of managing and provisioning infrastructure using machine-readable definition files instead of interactive or manual configuration. Treat the definitions as the source of truth: networks, virtual machines, storage, and security controls are declared, versioned, and executed. A helpful analogy is a building blueprint. A blueprint describes every wall, door, and electrical circuit so multiple builders can construct the same building consistently. Similarly, an IaC template is a blueprint for your cloud resources. It is executable: tools read the template and create or update resources so the runtime environment matches the specification. A concrete example is a Terraform module that defines a virtual network and a security group; running the module will produce the same network configuration every time. A common misconception is that IaC is only about speed; in fact, its primary security value is consistency and auditability. By keeping infrastructure in code you enable code review, automated checks, and rollback. Ask yourself: what would change in your environment if every manual infrastructure change needed an approved commit and a lint pass? What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)? means iac treats infrastructure as versioned, executable code — a blueprint that is deployable and testable.. In practical terms, a precise definition and a practical analogy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: IaC treats infrastructure as versioned, executable code — a blueprint that is deployable and testable.

content.html:
Definition
IaC is code that defines infrastructure and security settings

Like a blueprint for a building, IaC makes deployments repeatable and auditable. Versioning lets you review changes and rollback when needed.

Analogy
A blueprint reduces ambiguity for builders; IaC reduces ambiguity for operators and auditors by turning manual steps into a single executable specification.
Concrete example
A Terraform module that creates a subnet and security group. Each run produces the same network layout and access rules.
Misconception
IaC is not just automation speed

Speed is a benefit, but the security advantage comes from repeatability, versioning, and the ability to run automated checks before changes reach production.

Check your understanding
  • Can you name a configuration that should always be declared in IaC for your team?
  • How would you detect drift if a manual change occurs?

screens.title: How IaC Enforces Secure Configurations
screens.narratorSegment: IaC enforces secure configurations by making the desired state explicit and repeatable. The process begins with authoring a secure baseline in code that includes network rules, encryption settings, and service configurations. That file is stored in version control so changes require commits and reviews. Automated static analysis and linting scan templates for risky patterns. When deployments occur, a plan step previews the proposed changes and a CI pipeline runs tests and security scans. Finally, applying the IaC brings resources into the desired state; if drift occurs later, reapplying the same code returns resources to compliance. For example, if your baseline disables SSH on web servers and allows only HTTPS, any server missing that setting will be corrected when you re-run the template. A common pitfall is assuming the plan step is optional; skipping preview removes your chance to detect mistakes before they affect many resources. Consider how these stages reduce the chance of a single manual error becoming a fleet-wide exposure. How IaC Enforces Secure Configurations means author secure baselines, version them, lint and test, preview changes, then apply — re-run to remediate drift.. In practical terms, from baseline definition to automated remediation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Enforcement pipeline
keyIdea.text: Author secure baselines, version them, lint and test, preview changes, then apply — re-run to remediate drift.

content.html:
Process Steps
  1. Author secure baseline in IaC files and commit to version control.
  2. Run static analysis and linting to detect policy violations.
  3. Execute a plan/dry-run to preview changes and approvals.
  4. Apply changes through automation pipelines; monitor outcomes.
  5. Re-run templates to remediate any configuration drift.
Concrete scenario
Preventing an open SSH port across a fleet
Define a rule in the baseline that disallows SSH on web servers and requires HTTPS. Commit the change, run static checks, preview with plan, and apply. If a machine is misconfigured later, re-running the same code will restore compliance.
Key Takeaway

Making the desired state explicit enables automated enforcement and quick remediation of drift.

Common Mistake

Applying changes without a plan or skipping linting increases the risk of wide-impact misconfigurations.

screens.title: Terraform: Provisioning Secure Resources
screens.narratorSegment: Terraform is a provisioning tool used to create cloud resources across providers. Its strength for security is that network rules, IAM policies, and encryption settings are declared in HashiCorp Configuration Language so every run produces the same resources. In the provided HCL example we define an AWS security group that allows SSH only from a trusted CIDR and opens HTTPS to the internet. This explicit declaration prevents instances from inheriting permissive defaults. When using Terraform you should run terraform validate and incorporate static analysis such as Checkov or Terrascan to catch risky patterns. A common misconception is that Terraform alone enforces runtime configuration; Terraform provisions resources but does not configure software inside a server — that is where configuration management tools come in. Before applying, run terraform plan to preview the exact changes. After reviewing the plan, apply in a controlled pipeline to reduce blast radius. How could you limit the blast radius further? keyIdea.title: Terraform benefit
keyIdea.text: Declare provisioning-level security controls in HCL so resources are created with explicit, auditable rules.

content.html:
HCL Example
resource "aws_security_group" "web_server_sg" {
  name        = "web_server_sg"
  description = "Allow inbound SSH and outbound HTTPS"
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.main.id

  ingress {
    description = "SSH from trusted IP"
    from_port   = 22
    to_port     = 22
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["203.0.113.0/24"]
  }

  ingress {
    description = "HTTPS from anywhere"
    from_port   = 443
    to_port     = 443
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }

  tags = {
    Name = "Web Server Security Group"
  }
}
This HCL explicitly defines allowed inbound ports and source ranges, preventing permissive defaults.
Why this matters
Explicit rules reduce attack surface and ensure every instance created by this module receives the same network protections.
Tooling and checks
Run terraform validate and static analyzers such as Checkov or Terrascan as part of a CI pipeline to detect risky network or IAM patterns before apply.
Key Takeaway

Provisioning-level security belongs in IaC so created resources meet policy from day one.

screens.title: Ansible: Configuration Management and Hardening
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible is a configuration management tool used to apply software and settings to servers after they exist. Where Terraform creates the machine and network, Ansible makes sure the software and configuration inside that machine meet your security policies. The included playbook enforces SSH hardening: it ensures sshd is running, disables root login, and enforces public-key authentication. This is a practical hardening step applied across many hosts in a single run. Ansible’s strength is idempotent tasks that converge hosts to a known state. However, remember that Ansible needs secured credentials and a trusted control node. If those are compromised, an attacker could push changes widely. A misconception to correct is that configuration management replaces provisioning; both are complementary. Use Ansible to harden runtime configuration and Terraform to create the underlying resources. As a learner, try running linting on playbooks and using the check mode to preview actions safely. keyIdea.title: Ansible role
keyIdea.text: Use configuration management to apply hardening steps consistently across hosts after provisioning.

content.html:
Ansible Playbook
---
- name: Harden SSH configuration
  hosts: web_servers
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure SSH service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: sshd
        state: started
        enabled: true

    - name: Disable root login via SSH
      ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
        path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
        regexp: '^PermitRootLogin'
        line: 'PermitRootLogin no'
        state: present
      notify: restart sshd

    - name: Enforce PubkeyAuthentication
      ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
        path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
        regexp: '^PasswordAuthentication'
        line: 'PasswordAuthentication no'
        state: present
      notify: restart sshd

  handlers:
    - name: restart sshd
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: sshd
        state: restarted
This playbook is idempotent and will converge targets to the desired SSH configuration when run repeatedly.
How this helps security
Apply consistent hardening across hosts, reduce manual mistakes, and create an auditable change record for configuration updates.
Operational caution
Secure the control node and Ansible credentials. If those are compromised, the attacker can deploy changes to many systems.
Key Takeaway

Use Ansible to enforce runtime hardening, but protect the tooling and credentials as high-value assets.

screens.title: Provisioning vs Configuration Management
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning tools and configuration management tools each solve different problems and together form a secure deployment stack. Provisioning tools like Terraform create cloud resources: networks, subnets, load balancers, and IAM roles. Configuration management tools such as Ansible configure software and settings on those resources: packages, service configuration, user accounts, and security patches. The security distinction matters because some controls take effect at provisioning time — for example network ACLs and encryption at rest — and others are applied after a machine is created, such as disabling unwanted services. A common misconception is to treat one tool as a replacement for the other; instead, define provisioning-level guardrails in Terraform and enforce runtime hardening with Ansible. When designing a secure workflow, ensure both codebases are version-controlled, reviewed, and scanned by static analysis tools appropriate for their formats. Think about the right place to enforce a rule: should SSH be blocked by network rules or disabled inside the server? Often both answers apply for defense in depth. keyIdea.text: Terraform provisions infrastructure; Ansible configures and hardens systems. Use both and choose the correct layer for each control.

content.html:
Provisioning (Terraform)
What it does
  • Creates cloud resources and networks.
  • Declares IAM, security groups, and encryption settings.
  • Best for controls that must exist before a server runs.
Configuration (Ansible)
What it does
  • Installs packages, configures services, and hardens OS settings.
  • Applies idempotent tasks across existing hosts.
  • Best for runtime configuration and patching.
Design guidance
Use provisioning to enforce network- and identity-level security. Use configuration management to enforce OS and application-level hardening. For critical controls, implement both for defense in depth and ensure both code sets are reviewed and scanned.

screens.title: Securing the IaC Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Securing IaC is about protecting both the code and the pipeline that applies it. Start by storing IaC files in version control with restricted access and an audit trail. Require code review so security-aware reviewers can catch misconfigurations before merge. Add automated static analysis and linting: terraform validate, ansible-lint, and scanning tools such as Checkov or Terrascan will surface policy violations. Use branching and pull request workflows to separate proposed changes until they pass checks. Apply the principle of least privilege to the identities used by your IaC tooling: service accounts should have only the permissions needed to create the specified resources. Never hardcode secrets into templates; instead, reference a dedicated secrets manager. Finally, integrate plan and dry-run steps into CI so humans and automated checks can review planned changes. A common mistake is treating IaC repositories like documentation — if it’s executable, it must be treated with the same security rigor as application code to limit blast radius. screens.narratorSegment: While IaC reduces many risks, it also centralizes them: IaC artifacts and pipelines become high-value targets. If an attacker alters a template or gains control of the CI pipeline, they can propagate misconfiguration across many resources instantly. screens.title: Immutable Infrastructure
screens.narratorSegment: Immutable infrastructure is an approach where servers are not modified in place; instead, new hardened images are built and deployed, and old instances are decommissioned. From a security perspective, this reduces configuration drift because every deployed instance originates from the same validated image. fullNarratorScript:
Infrastructure as Code is the practice of describing your network, servers, and security settings in machine-readable files so infrastructure is repeatable, versioned, and testable. In this lesson you will learn why IaC replaces error-prone manual setup with a predictable, auditable process and how that matters for cybersecurity. We’ll look at two complementary tool families: provisioning tools that create cloud resources and configuration tools that harden software on servers. You will see concrete examples — a Terraform security group that restricts SSH, and an Ansible playbook that hardens SSH configuration. I’ll also highlight common mistakes to avoid: storing secrets in code, granting overly broad permissions, and skipping linting or code review. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain how IaC enforces a secure baseline, why immutable infrastructure reduces drift, and which controls protect your IaC workflow. Consider how version control plus automated checks could have prevented a past misconfiguration in your environment; that perspective will help you apply these practices.

In this chapter you will gain four practical competencies. First, you will be able to explain what Infrastructure as Code is and why it improves security posture. That includes defining machine-readable infrastructure and recognizing how versioning brings repeatability. Second, you will identify how IaC enforces secure configurations and prevents configuration drift by repeatedly applying a known, tested baseline. You’ll see concrete examples like disallowing SSH or enforcing HTTPS. Third, you will describe the roles of provisioning and configuration tools — for example, Terraform for resource creation and Ansible for hardening servers — and how they connect to security controls like IAM, security groups, and encryption. Fourth, you will recognize common IaC security challenges and apply best practices: secure repositories, mandatory code reviews, static analysis tooling, least-privilege service accounts, secrets management, and immutable infrastructure. These objectives leave you prepared to review IaC templates for security issues and to design safe deployment workflows. Think about a recent misconfiguration you’ve seen and how each objective would reduce that risk.

Beyond understanding, this chapter gives you practice tasks that mirror real operations. You will read and reason about Terraform HCL that creates cloud resources and about Ansible playbooks that enforce hardening. You will practice running static checks such as Terraform validate and Ansible lint to catch misconfigurations early. You will also practice creating minimal permission identities for IaC tools so service accounts only have what they need. Finally, you will run safe previews: a terraform plan and Ansible's check mode to verify intent without applying changes. These skills build operational confidence and reduce the likelihood of sweeping, accidental changes. As you practice, consider two common pitfalls: treating IaC as documentation rather than executable code, and storing secrets in plain text. Your exercises will focus on detection and prevention so IaC becomes part of a secure, auditable pipeline.

Infrastructure as Code is the practice of managing and provisioning infrastructure using machine-readable definition files instead of interactive or manual configuration. Treat the definitions as the source of truth: networks, virtual machines, storage, and security controls are declared, versioned, and executed. A helpful analogy is a building blueprint. A blueprint describes every wall, door, and electrical circuit so multiple builders can construct the same building consistently. Similarly, an IaC template is a blueprint for your cloud resources. It is executable: tools read the template and create or update resources so the runtime environment matches the specification. A concrete example is a Terraform module that defines a virtual network and a security group; running the module will produce the same network configuration every time. A common misconception is that IaC is only about speed; in fact, its primary security value is consistency and auditability. By keeping infrastructure in code you enable code review, automated checks, and rollback. Ask yourself: what would change in your environment if every manual infrastructure change needed an approved commit and a lint pass? What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)? means iac treats infrastructure as versioned, executable code — a blueprint that is deployable and testable.. In practical terms, a precise definition and a practical analogy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IaC enforces secure configurations by making the desired state explicit and repeatable. The process begins with authoring a secure baseline in code that includes network rules, encryption settings, and service configurations. That file is stored in version control so changes require commits and reviews. Automated static analysis and linting scan templates for risky patterns. When deployments occur, a plan step previews the proposed changes and a CI pipeline runs tests and security scans. Finally, applying the IaC brings resources into the desired state; if drift occurs later, reapplying the same code returns resources to compliance. For example, if your baseline disables SSH on web servers and allows only HTTPS, any server missing that setting will be corrected when you re-run the template. A common pitfall is assuming the plan step is optional; skipping preview removes your chance to detect mistakes before they affect many resources. Consider how these stages reduce the chance of a single manual error becoming a fleet-wide exposure. How IaC Enforces Secure Configurations means author secure baselines, version them, lint and test, preview changes, then apply — re-run to remediate drift.. In practical terms, from baseline definition to automated remediation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Terraform is a provisioning tool used to create cloud resources across providers. Its strength for security is that network rules, IAM policies, and encryption settings are declared in HashiCorp Configuration Language so every run produces the same resources. In the provided HCL example we define an AWS security group that allows SSH only from a trusted CIDR and opens HTTPS to the internet. This explicit declaration prevents instances from inheriting permissive defaults. When using Terraform you should run terraform validate and incorporate static analysis such as Checkov or Terrascan to catch risky patterns. A common misconception is that Terraform alone enforces runtime configuration; Terraform provisions resources but does not configure software inside a server — that is where configuration management tools come in. Before applying, run terraform plan to preview the exact changes. After reviewing the plan, apply in a controlled pipeline to reduce blast radius. How could you limit the blast radius further? Consider module-level defaults and least-privilege IAM roles for the tool itself. Terraform: Provisioning Secure Resources means declare provisioning-level security controls in hcl so resources are created with explicit, auditable rules.. In practical terms, hcl example that defines a security group and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ansible is a configuration management tool used to apply software and settings to servers after they exist. Where Terraform creates the machine and network, Ansible makes sure the software and configuration inside that machine meet your security policies. The included playbook enforces SSH hardening: it ensures sshd is running, disables root login, and enforces public-key authentication. This is a practical hardening step applied across many hosts in a single run. Ansible’s strength is idempotent tasks that converge hosts to a known state. However, remember that Ansible needs secured credentials and a trusted control node. If those are compromised, an attacker could push changes widely. A misconception to correct is that configuration management replaces provisioning; both are complementary. Use Ansible to harden runtime configuration and Terraform to create the underlying resources. As a learner, try running linting on playbooks and using the check mode to preview actions safely. Ansible: Configuration Management and Hardening means use configuration management to apply hardening steps consistently across hosts after provisioning.. In practical terms, yaml playbook example to enforce ssh hardening. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Provisioning tools and configuration management tools each solve different problems and together form a secure deployment stack. Provisioning tools like Terraform create cloud resources: networks, subnets, load balancers, and IAM roles. Configuration management tools such as Ansible configure software and settings on those resources: packages, service configuration, user accounts, and security patches. The security distinction matters because some controls take effect at provisioning time — for example network ACLs and encryption at rest — and others are applied after a machine is created, such as disabling unwanted services. A common misconception is to treat one tool as a replacement for the other; instead, define provisioning-level guardrails in Terraform and enforce runtime hardening with Ansible. When designing a secure workflow, ensure both codebases are version-controlled, reviewed, and scanned by static analysis tools appropriate for their formats. Think about the right place to enforce a rule: should SSH be blocked by network rules or disabled inside the server? Often both answers apply for defense in depth. Provisioning vs Configuration Management means terraform provisions infrastructure; ansible configures and hardens systems. use both and choose the correct layer for each control.. In practical terms, how terraform and ansible complement each other for security. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Securing IaC is about protecting both the code and the pipeline that applies it. Start by storing IaC files in version control with restricted access and an audit trail. Require code review so security-aware reviewers can catch misconfigurations before merge. Add automated static analysis and linting: terraform validate, ansible-lint, and scanning tools such as Checkov or Terrascan will surface policy violations. Use branching and pull request workflows to separate proposed changes until they pass checks. Apply the principle of least privilege to the identities used by your IaC tooling: service accounts should have only the permissions needed to create the specified resources.
